claims.claim: In the end, every soul will be saved.

stances.summary: Christ the Word will in the end win over every reasoning creature and heal every soul. No evil in a soul is too strong for God to cure, though the cure may take ages.
stances.quote: But our belief is, that the Word shall prevail over the entire rational creation, and change every soul into His own perfection; in which state every one, by the mere exercise of his power, will choose what he desires, and obtain what he chooses.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 248, late in his life, and preserved in Greek (not in Rufinus's Latin). The same chapter goes on: 'we hold that in the mind there is no evil so strong that it may not be overcome by the Supreme Word and God', and calls the goal 'the total destruction of evil, and the restoration to righteousness of every soul', but declines to say whether evil could arise again. On First Principles (about 220-230, surviving mainly in Rufinus's admittedly smoothed Latin) says the same: 'We think, indeed, that the goodness of God, through His Christ, may recall all His creatures to one end, even His enemies being conquered and subdued' (1.6.1, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04121.htm) and speaks of the time 'When, therefore, all rational souls shall have been restored' (3.6.6, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04123.htm). HEDGES: he calls this discussion 'investigation and discussion, than ... fixed and certain decision' (1.6.1); he leaves the fate of the devil's angels to the reader (1.6.3); in Against Celsus 6.26 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04166.htm) he says it is dangerous to write about this because 'the multitude need no further instruction than that which relates to the punishment of sinners'. In a letter to friends in Alexandria (about 231, quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 2.18, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/27102.htm) he denies teaching 'that the father of wickedness and perdition of those who shall be cast out of the kingdom of God can be saved; a thing which not even a madman can say'; Jerome replies (2.19) that in his debate with Candidus Origen had argued the devil fell by his own will 'and can be saved'. Scholars still dispute what he finally held. HETERODOX STATUS: never condemned for this in his lifetime; his teaching on the restoration of all was condemned by Justinian's edict of 543 and in the anti-Origenist anathemas linked to the Council of Constantinople of 553. Augustine (City of God 21.17) says the Church 'not without reason' condemned him for extending release even to the devil.

stances.summary: Punishment after death is a painful cure, like fire refining gold. When evil has been burned out of everyone, even the devil, the whole creation will give thanks together.
stances.quote: when, after long periods of time, the evil of our nature, which now is mixed up with it and has grown with its growth, has been expelled, and when there has been a restoration of those who are now lying in Sin to their primal state, a harmony of thanksgiving will arise from all creation
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: Written about 385 as a handbook for teachers of the faith. The same chapter ends by saying that Christ's work is 'freeing both man from evil, and healing even the introducer of evil himself. For the chastisement, however painful, of moral disease is a healing of its weakness.' Chapter 35 (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf205.xi.ii.xxxvii.html) sends the unbaptized and unrepentant to the furnace 'in order that, the vice which has been mixed up in them being melted away after long succeeding ages, their nature may be restored pure again to God.' Chapter 40 (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf205.xi.ii.xlii.html), however, says of the fire of the next life that 'that fire is never quenched' and speaks of the worm that 'dieth not', which believers in eternal punishment quote. A scribe wrote in the margin of one manuscript of chapter 26 that it 'seems to savour of Origen's opinion' (Krabinger, cited in the NPNF note). On the Soul and the Resurrection gives the same teaching to his sister Macrina. Never condemned; venerated as a saint in East and West. Note: the NPNF page on CCEL prints footnotes inline, so the checker should expect a footnote number ('2007') straight after the quotation.

stances.summary: God has one goal: to bring the whole human race, from the first man to the last, into His blessings. Some are cleansed in this life and some later by a healing fire, but in the end evil will have nowhere left to live.
stances.quote: His end is one, and one only; it is this: when the complete whole of our race shall have been perfected from the first man to the last — some having at once in this life been cleansed from evil, others having afterwards in the necessary periods been healed by the Fire
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection (a dialogue written by her brother Gregory of Nyssa)
stances.location: Macrina's reply to Gregory's objections about the resurrection, late in the dialogue (paragraph beginning 'As to the how and the when of his dissolution')
stances.context: Gregory wrote the dialogue about 380-381, recounting what his sister (died 379) said on her deathbed; she is 'the Teacher'. Her words reach us through him and may be shaped by him. Earlier in the dialogue she argues that 'when it shall be that every will rests in God, evil will be reduced to complete annihilation, owing to no receptacle being left for it', and that the fire lasts longer or shorter according to the amount of evil in each person. The sentence continues: 'to offer to every one of us participation in the blessings which are in Him'. Venerated as a saint.

stances.summary: The Lord saves all: some follow Him willingly, others are turned by punishments, so that every knee will bow to Him. God's punishments are meant to heal and to bring repentance.
stances.quote: He, indeed, saves all; but some [He saves], converting them by punishments; others, however, who follow voluntarily [He saves] with dignity of honour; so that every knee should bow to Him, of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Comments on the First Epistle of John (the Adumbrations)
stances.context: About 200. This survives only in a 6th-century Latin digest made for Cassiodorus, not in Clement's Greek, so the wording is at one remove. The same comments (on 1 John 1:5) say God 'destroys no one, but gives salvation to all'. Stromata 7.2 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02107.htm): 'all things are arranged with a view to the salvation of the universe by the Lord of the universe'. Stromata 6.6 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02106.htm): 'God's punishments are saving and disciplinary, leading to conversion'. QUALIFICATIONS: the same chapter of Stromata 6 allows that souls who hear the gospel in Hades 'might either exhibit repentance, or confess that their punishment was just', and Who Is the Rich Man 33 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0207.htm) warns of 'the punishment of eternal fire'. So he leans toward correction for all but never states it as flatly as Origen. Never condemned.

stances.summary: (Early, and disputed.) In the restoration of all things Christ the physician will heal the whole torn body, and every creature will become again what God made it, even the fallen angel.
stances.quote: for instance, that the apostate angel shall begin to be that which he was by his creation, and that man who had been cast out of paradise shall be restored again to the cultivation of paradise
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, 1892 (Jerome quoting his own commentary)
stances.work: Commentary on Ephesians (on Ephesians 4:16), as quoted by Jerome himself in his Apology against Rufinus
stances.context: The commentary was written in Bethlehem about 386-388 and leans heavily on Origen's lost commentary. The passage opens: 'And so in the restitution of all things, when Jesus Christ the true physician comes to restore to health the whole body of the Church ... every one will receive his proper place'. Rufinus (Apology 1.42) held it up as Jerome's own Origenism. Jerome answered in 401-402 (same section and 1.27) that he had 'summed up in a short sentence Origen's exposition' and 'quoted Origen's views as, According to another heresy'. Whether it was ever his own belief is disputed; do not present it as his settled view. CHANGE OF MIND: by 399 he rejected it outright (next entry).

stances.summary: God answers sinners with grace, not strict justice: He raises them and clothes even those who trampled His laws in glory. Hell itself is the pain of love felt by those who sinned against love.
stances.quote: The retribution of the sinners is this, that He repays them with resurrection instead of with justice. And those that have trampled upon His laws are clad by Him with the glory of perfection instead of with the body.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923)
stances.work: Mystic Treatises (the First Part of his writings)
stances.location: Treatise 50 in Wensinck's numbering ('Short sections containing various considerations...'), p. 241
stances.context: Isaac, briefly bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East, wrote in Syriac in the late 7th century and is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox Church. The same passage asks: 'Where is Hell which can make us suffer?' Treatise 27 (p. 136): 'Also I say that even those who are scourged in Hell are tormented with the scourgings of love.' His explicit teaching that Gehenna will come to an end is in his Second Part (chapters 39-41), found in 1983 and available in English only in Sebastian Brock's copyrighted translation (1995), so it is not quoted here. The Book of the Bee (13th century; Budge's translation, 1886, chapter 60, https://archive.org/download/bookofbee00solo/bookofbee00solo_djvu.txt) quotes 'Mar Isaac': 'In the world which is to come grace will be the judge and not justice.' Note for the checker: the archive.org text is OCR; the scan's OCR misreads the title-page year as 1933, but the book appeared in 1923.

stances.summary: The good receive a lasting reward, but sinners are punished only for a short time, in proportion to their sins, and then share in unending happiness. God's mercy far outweighs the penalty.
stances.quote: A lasting reward, which is worthy of the justice of the Giver, is laid up for the good, in return for their labours ; and torment for sinners, but not everlasting, that the immortality which is prepared for them may not be worthless.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Book of the Bee (Oxford, 1886)
stances.work: Book of the Dispensation (lost), quoted by Solomon of Basra in The Book of the Bee
stances.location: The Book of the Bee, chapter 60, pp. 140-141
stances.context: Diodore (died about 390), bishop of Tarsus, was the teacher of John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia. The line survives only in this quotation by a 13th-century bishop of the Church of the East; the work itself is lost, so it cannot be checked against Diodore's own text. The quotation continues: 'it is not for the good only that the grace of the resurrection from the dead is intended, but also for the wicked'. Diodore was attacked after his death as a forerunner of Nestorius, for his teaching on Christ, not for this. The spaced semicolon ('labours ;') is how the 1886 book prints it. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: The wicked, once their minds are set right by penalties, will choose the good and be admitted to God's generosity. Christ's words about paying the last penny, and about few or many stripes, show that punishment comes to an end.
stances.quote: For He would never have said, “ Until thou payest the uttermost farthing,” unless it had been possible for us to be freed from our sins through having atoned for them by paying the penalty
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Book of the Bee (Oxford, 1886)
stances.work: From his writings, quoted by Solomon of Basra in The Book of the Bee
stances.location: The Book of the Bee, chapter 60, p. 140
stances.context: Theodore (about 350-428), bishop of Mopsuestia, honoured as the Interpreter in the Church of the East. Preserved only as this 13th-century quotation; the Bee adds that 'the Expositor has handed down in his books clearly and distinctly' these views. He was condemned after his death in 553 (the Three Chapters), for his teaching on Christ. The odd spacing inside the quotation marks is how the scan prints it. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Whoever corrupts the faith with false teaching goes into the fire that never ends, and so does whoever follows him.
stances.quote: Such an one becoming defiled [in this way], shall go away into everlasting fire, and so shall every one that hearkens unto him.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 107-110 on his way to martyrdom in Rome. The Greek has 'the unquenchable fire'. A warning in passing, not an argument about how long punishment lasts.

stances.summary: Christ will judge the wicked, raised in their bodies, and punish them forever, not for a limited term as Plato taught.
stances.quote: we say that the same thing will be done, but at the hand of Christ, and upon the wicked in the same bodies united again to their spirits which are now to undergo everlasting punishment; and not only, as Plato said, for a period of a thousand years.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: About 155, addressed to the emperor. Chapter 28 repeats it: the devil 'would be sent into the fire with his host, and the men who follow him, and would be punished for an endless duration'. In the Dialogue with Trypho 5 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01281.htm) an old man tells Justin that some souls 'are punished so long as God wills them to exist and to be punished'; that is the old man's line in the story, sometimes read as a hint that the wicked might one day cease to exist. Martyred about 165.

stances.summary: Those who reject the Word of God and turn back from Him receive a punishment that is not temporary but eternal.
stances.quote: thus also the punishment of those who do not believe the Word of God, and despise His advent, and are turned away backwards, is increased; being not merely temporal, but rendered also eternal.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: About 180. The passage goes on: 'these shall be damned for ever'. In his summary of the Church's rule of faith (1.10.1, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103110.htm) he quotes 'every knee should bow' (Philippians 2:10, the verse universalists lean on) and in the same sentence says Christ will send the rebel angels and the wicked 'into everlasting fire'.

stances.summary: After the resurrection the servants of God live with Him forever, and the wicked are handed over to a fire that burns without ever consuming them.
stances.quote: but the profane, and all who are not true worshippers of God, in like manner shall be consigned to the punishment of everlasting fire— that fire which, from its very nature indeed, directly ministers to their incorruptibility.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Written about 197, before his Montanist years. The same chapter: 'A notable proof this of the fire eternal!' On the Spectacles 30 (about 200, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0303.htm) pictures persecuting governors, philosophers and actors burning at the last judgment, 'that last day of judgment, with its everlasting issues', as the Christian's true show.

stances.summary: Knowing the true God is how a person escapes the eternal lake of fire and the worm that never stops.
stances.quote: You shall escape the boiling flood of hell's eternal lake of fire and the eye ever fixed in menacing glare of fallen angels chained in Tartarus as punishment for their sins
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.location: Book 10, chapter 30 in ANF (chapter 34 in modern editions)
stances.context: The closing appeal to pagans, about 225. The work is traditionally given to Hippolytus, but the authorship is debated. The raw page has a double space after 'hell's' (a removed footnote mark).

stances.summary: Hell burns forever and gives the condemned neither rest nor end. Life is won or lost here, because after death there is no more room for repentance.
stances.quote: An ever-burning Gehenna will burn up the condemned, and a punishment devouring with living flames; nor will there be any source whence at any time they may have either respite or end to their torments.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: About 252, addressed to a pagan official who blamed Christians for plague and famine. Section 25: 'When you have once departed there, there is no longer any place for repentance, and no possibility of making satisfaction. Here life is either lost or saved'.

stances.summary: The wicked will be raised in bodies that cannot be destroyed, and a divine fire will burn them forever while renewing what it burns.
stances.quote: The same divine fire, therefore, with one and the same force and power, will both burn the wicked and will form them again, and will replace as much as it shall consume of their bodies, and will supply itself with eternal nourishment
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written about 304-311. The same chapter says the righteous too will be tried by fire: those with many or heavy sins will be scorched, while the fully just 'will not perceive that fire'. So a testing fire for believers, but endless burning for the wicked.

stances.summary: Everyone will rise in an eternal body. The sinner's body is made to endure punishment, burning forever without being consumed.
stances.quote: but if a man is a sinner, he shall receive an eternal body, fitted to endure the penalties of sins, that he may burn eternally in fire, nor ever be consumed.
stances.translation: Edwin Hamilton Gifford, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Instruction for people about to be baptized, Jerusalem, about 350. Not in the candidate pool; recorded to show the ordinary teaching given to new Christians.

stances.summary: Christ calls both the punishment and the life 'eternal', so if one ends, the other would too. The idea that hell ends is a trick of the devil to make people sin more boldly.
stances.quote: But if we cannot think this of life, with what reason shall we give eternal punishment an end? For both equally have the adjective eternal.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK, 1925)
stances.context: From the monastic rules Basil wrote in the 360s-370s, in question-and-answer form. The question asks how some can say there is no end of punishment, since Scripture says one man is beaten with many stripes and another with few (Luke 12:47-48). Basil answers that the stripes show a difference in the punishment, not an end to it, and that 'this comes also from the devil’s plots that many men, forgetting such great and serious words and declarations of the Lord, assign to themselves an end of punishment' so that 'they may sin more boldly'. (The OCR prints a stray margin letter 'B' before 'they may sin', and misreads 'is' as '1s' in the question, so only short stretches are quoted here.) Clarke notes that the question and first sentence of the answer are quoted by Justinian in his letter to Menas (543), in the case against Origenism. The archive.org text is OCR.

stances.summary: There is a cleansing fire that Christ came to bring, and there is an avenging fire, eternal for the wicked. Yet he leaves the door open for those who read even that fire more mercifully.
stances.quote: and one even more fearful still than these, the unquenchable fire which is ranged with the worm that dies not but is eternal for the wicked. For all these belong to the destroying power; though some may prefer even in this place to take a more merciful view of this fire, worthily of Him That chastises.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached at Constantinople in 381. He states the eternal fire but pointedly does not rule out a gentler reading. In Oration 39.19 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310239.htm), of the Novatianist schismatics: 'Perhaps in it they will be baptized with Fire, in that last Baptism which is more painful and longer, which devours wood like grass', a purifying fire after death for some outside the Church. The raw page has double spaces after 'fire' and 'view' (removed footnote marks).

stances.summary: Many comfort themselves that hell is milder than threatened and only temporary. It is not: Paul calls it eternal destruction, and what is everlasting cannot be temporary.
stances.quote: But that it is not temporary, hear Paul now saying, concerning those who know not God, and who do not believe in the Gospel, that they shall suffer punishment, even eternal destruction. How then is that temporary which is everlasting?
stances.translation: John A. Broadus, NPNF 1st series vol. 13, 1889
stances.context: The homily opens: 'There are many men, who form good hopes not by abstaining from their sins, but by thinking that hell is not so terrible as it is said to be, but milder than what is threatened, and temporary, not eternal; and about this they philosophize much.' In Homily 9 on First Corinthians (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220109.htm) he reads Paul's 'saved, yet so as by fire' as meaning the opposite of release: 'as if he had said, But himself shall remain forever in punishment.' Bishop of Constantinople 398-404.

stances.summary: The devil and his angels, and those who do his work, will have their portion in the eternal fire. Whoever denies it deserves to learn it by experience.
stances.quote: If then any one denies that the devil is to be subjected to the eternal fires, may he have his part with him in the eternal fire, so that he may know by experience the fact which he now denies.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, 1892
stances.work: Apology to Anastasius, Bishop of Rome
stances.context: Written about 400 to clear himself of Origenism after he translated Origen's On First Principles into Latin. A profession made under suspicion: Jerome (Apology against Rufinus 2.6-7) mocked it and hinted that Rufinus still took 'eternal fires' in Origen's sense, as the torment of conscience. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: (Later view.) Hoping that even the devil will one day repent is a vain hope that drags people to hell. Life must be won or lost here.
stances.quote: Let us not wait for the repentance of the devil; for this is a vain anticipation and one that will drag us into the deep of hell. Life must be sought or lost here.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 399-400 in the Origenist quarrel. CHANGE OF MIND: the same section says 'In youth we have wandered; now that we are old let us mend our ways' and 'imitate my penitence'. Section 7 rejects a 'restitution of all things' in which 'it will be the same for Gabriel as for the devil, for Paul as for Caiaphas'. Letter 124 to Avitus (about 409, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001124.htm) lists Origen's teaching that demons may be restored among the passages that 'deserve the church's condemnation'. Compare his earlier commentary on Ephesians (previous Jerome entry).

stances.summary: Christ said 'eternal punishment' and 'eternal life' in the same breath. If one never ends, neither does the other; kind hearts cannot soften His words.
stances.quote: And to say in one and the same sense, life eternal shall be endless, punishment eternal shall come to an end, is the height of absurdity. Wherefore, as the eternal life of the saints shall be endless, so too the eternal punishment of those who are doomed to it shall have no end.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF 1st series vol. 2, 1887
stances.original: Dicere autem in hoc uno eodemque sensu: "Vita aeterna sine fine erit, supplicium aeternum finem habebit" multum absurdum est. Vnde, quia uita aeterna sanctorum sine fine erit, supplicium quoque aeternum quibus erit finem procul dubio non habebit.
stances.context: Book 21 was written about 426. Chapter 17 argues, 'amicably', with 'those tender-hearted Christians' who think the damned will be freed after a fixed term, and with Origen, who extended release to the devil; chapters 18-27 answer narrower hopes (release through the saints' prayers, or for all the baptized, or all Catholics, or all who gave alms). In the Enchiridion 112 (about 421, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1302.htm) he says 'some, indeed very many' lament eternal punishment, and lets them suppose the pains are 'at certain intervals, in some degree assuaged', but never ended. Latin from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/civ21.shtml).

stances.summary: On judgment day the ungodly and sinners will not be spared but will burn in eternal fire, as the Gospel says. Anyone who believes otherwise is following Origen.
stances.quote: In the day of judgment no forbearance will be shown to the ungodly and the sinners, but they will be consumed in eternal fires.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes and Robert Ernest Wallis, revised by Benjamin B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5, 1887
stances.work: His book of Chapters, as read out at the Synod of Diospolis and recorded by Augustine in On the Proceedings of Pelagius
stances.location: On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapters 9-10
stances.context: Read out against him at the Synod of Diospolis (Lydda) in December 415. He defended it from Matthew 25:46 and added, 'Who believes differently is an Origenist' (chapter 10), which the bishops approved. Augustine (writing in 417) objects only that the line seems to leave no room for Christians 'saved, yet so as by fire'. HETERODOX: Pelagius was later condemned (Carthage 418, Ephesus 431) for his teaching on grace, not for this.

stances.summary: No one who truly repents is beyond God's mercy, not even the devil. If he stopped attacking people and repented, Martin would promise him the mercy of Christ.
stances.quote: If you, yourself, wretched being, would but desist from attacking mankind, and even, at this period, when the day of judgment is at hand, would only repent of your deeds, I, with a true confidence in the Lord, would promise you the mercy of Christ.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.work: Life of St Martin, by Sulpicius Severus
stances.context: Sulpicius knew Martin and wrote about 396, while Martin was still alive; this story came from 'some of the brethren', and Sulpicius writes 'Martin is said to have cried out'. It arose when a demon mocked Martin for readmitting fallen monks. A conditional offer, not a prediction that all will be saved; Sulpicius calls it 'a holy boldness' in which Martin 'could not assert authority'.

stances.summary: We must obey God now, so that He never has to hand us over to everlasting punishment as servants who refused to follow Him to glory.
stances.quote: that not only may He never, as an angry father, disinherit His children, but may never, as a dreadful Lord, incensed by our sins, deliver us to everlasting punishment, as most wicked servants who would not follow Him to glory.
stances.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd edition (Fort Augustus, 1906)
stances.original: ut non solum, ut iratus pater, non aliquando filios suos exhaeredet; sed nec, ut metuendus Dominus, irritatus malis nostris, ut nequissimos servos, perpetuam tradat ad poenam qui eum sequi noluerint ad gloriam.
stances.context: Written about 530-540. In passing, not argued. Chapter 4 lists among the tools of good works 'To fear the Day of Judgment' and 'To be in dread of hell' (Latin 'Diem judicii timere', 'Gehennam expavescere'). The Latin is printed facing the English in the same scan; the archive.org text is OCR.

stances.summary: After death some penalties simply punish, while others are merciful and cleanse. He does not say more.
stances.quote: great are these penalties, some of them inflicted, I imagine, in the severity of retribution, others in the mercy of purification.
stances.translation: H. R. James, The Consolation of Philosophy (1897)
stances.context: Written about 524 in prison, awaiting execution. Lady Philosophy is speaking, in reply to Boethius asking about 'the punishment of the soul after the death of the body'; she adds 'But it is not my present purpose to speak of these.' The book argues in philosophical rather than openly Christian terms. Some punishment heals and some does not; he does not say whether the retributive kind ends. Weak evidence; use with care.

stances.summary: Just as the joy of the good never ends, the torment of the wicked never ends. God takes no pleasure in it, but He is just, and the wicked would have gone on sinning forever if they could.
stances.quote: Certain it is, and without all doubt most true, that as the good shall have no end of their joys, so the wicked never any release of their torments
stances.translation: 'P.W.' (1608), re-edited by Edmund G. Gardner (London, 1911)
stances.location: Book 4, chapter 44 ('whether those that be in hell shall burn there for ever')
stances.context: Written 593-594. The chapter is a direct answer to the question. When his deacon Peter asks how a sin that ended can be punished without end, Gregory replies that the wicked 'would, had it been in their power, have lived without end, that they might in like manner have sinned without end'. Also: 'Almighty God, because he is merciful and full of pity, taketh no pleasure in the torments of wretched men: but because he is also just, therefore doth he never give over to punish the wicked.' Chapter 39 of the same book accepts 'a Purgatory fire for certain small sins' before the judgment, which is a different question.

splits_fathers: Most early Christians whose writings survive taught that punishment for the unrepentant never ends: Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Lactantius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Basil, Chrysostom, Augustine, the later Jerome, Pelagius, Benedict and Gregory the Great. But there are real, named voices on the other side, and they are serious figures, not fringe ones: Origen, Gregory of Nyssa and his sister Macrina, Isaac the Syrian, and (as quoted later) Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, with Clement of Alexandria leaning that way. Gregory of Nazianzus deliberately left the question open, and Martin of Tours offered mercy even to the devil if he repented. The mainstream writers themselves say the hopeful view was common among ordinary believers: Basil says 'many men' assign themselves an end of punishment, Chrysostom says 'There are many men' who think hell 'temporary, not eternal', and Augustine speaks of 'some, indeed very many'. The restoration of all, in Origen's form, was condemned by Justinian in 543 and in the anathemas linked to the Council of 553. So the claim splits the Fathers well: a clear majority against, a respected minority for, and a few in between. A player who agrees lands near Origen, Nyssa, Macrina or Isaac; a player who disagrees lands near Augustine, Basil, Chrysostom or Gregory the Great.
splits_people_today: It divides people well. Most Christian churches teach officially that hell is real and final (Catholic, Orthodox and confessional Protestant teaching all say so), and most evangelicals hold it firmly; a minority of evangelicals hold instead that the lost are finally destroyed rather than saved. Yet many Christians hope that all will be saved, and the hope has well-known defenders: Hans Urs von Balthasar's book Dare We Hope among Catholics, Rob Bell's Love Wins (2011) and David Bentley Hart's That All Shall Be Saved (2019). Many people who do not go to church reject hell altogether, and say a loving God would not punish forever. Others, religious or not, feel that justice requires the worst evil (the usual example is Hitler) to meet a final reckoning. Pew surveys have found that clearly fewer Americans say they believe in hell than in heaven (roughly six in ten against seven in ten or more), and belief in hell is much lower in Britain and Western Europe. The words 'every soul' sharpen the split, because they include the worst people who ever lived.

misattributions.line: Jerome's commentary on Ephesians, 'the apostate angel shall begin to be that which he was by his creation', cited as Jerome's own belief in universal restoration.
misattributions.truth: The words are in his Commentary on Ephesians (386-388), but Jerome said in 401-402 that he was summarizing Origen and comparing two heresies (Apology against Rufinus 1.26-27), and in 399 he wrote 'Let us not wait for the repentance of the devil' (Letter 84.6). At best an early view he disowned; at worst never his view.

misattributions.line: Basil admitted that most Christians of his day believed hell would end.
misattributions.truth: Shorter Rules 267 says 'many men' assign themselves an end of punishment through 'the devil’s plots' so that 'they may sin more boldly'. It shows the view was common enough to answer, not that it was the majority, and Basil condemns it.

misattributions.line: Augustine admitted that 'very many' in his day believed in universal salvation.
misattributions.truth: Enchiridion 112 does say 'some, indeed very many' lament eternal punishment and soften the texts. But in City of God 21.17-27 the 'tender-hearted' views he describes are mostly partial ones (release for the baptized, for Catholics, for alms-givers, through the saints' prayers), and he argues against them all. It is evidence of a widespread hope, not of a majority universalist Church.

misattributions.line: Justin Martyr taught that the wicked are punished only for as long as God wills, not forever.
misattributions.truth: The line 'others are punished so long as God wills them to exist and to be punished' (Dialogue with Trypho 5) is spoken by the old man who converts Justin in the story. In his own voice Justin says 'everlasting punishment' and 'an endless duration' (First Apology 8 and 28).

misattributions.line: 'He, indeed, saves all' quoted as Clement of Alexandria's own Greek words.
misattributions.truth: Real, but it survives only in a 6th-century Latin digest (the Adumbrations) made for Cassiodorus, not in Clement's Greek. Quote it with that caution.

notes: 1) Four positions existed, not two: punishment forever (the majority); restoration of all, sometimes including the devil (Origen, Nyssa, Isaac); a purifying fire for some believers while the wicked burn forever (Lactantius, Gregory the Great's purgatory for small sins, Augustine's 'saved, yet so as by fire'); and hopes of release for the baptized or for Catholics, which Augustine answers in City of God 21.18-27. The claim that every soul will be saved only fits the second. 2) Both sides argued from the same verses: the universalists from 'God will be all in all' (1 Corinthians 15:28) and 'every knee should bow' (Philippians 2:10); the others from Matthew 25:46, where Basil and Augustine insist 'eternal' must mean the same for punishment and life, while Diodore and Theodore (in the Book of the Bee) argue that 'eternal' is not definite. 3) Not recorded, though relevant: Evagrius Ponticus and Didymus the Blind taught Origen's restoration and were condemned with him in 553, but their works survive in English only in modern copyrighted translations. Isaac's plainest chapters (Second Part, chapters 39-41) are likewise only in Brock's 1995 translation. 4) Perpetua's vision of her dead brother Dinocrates is about prayer for the dead, not universal salvation; do not use it for this claim. 5) No clear statement either way was found in this pass for Athanasius, Ephrem, Hilary, Ambrose, Antony, the desert mothers and fathers, Cassian, Paulinus, Climacus or Novatian. 6) The anti-Origenist anathemas are commonly credited to the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553). Scholars debate whether that council formally enacted them or whether they were passed at a meeting just before it opened; either way they were issued with Justinian's backing. 7) Later Byzantine writers (Germanus of Constantinople, as reported by Photius) claimed Origenists had tampered with Gregory of Nyssa's books, and Maximus the Confessor reread his 'restoration' as the healing of the soul's powers; this was not checked in this pass, and most scholars read the passages as Gregory's own. 8) Display: several public-domain translations here print pronouns for God in lower case (Gregory the Great's 1608 English: 'he is merciful'). The site's rule capitalizes them, but the machine check must use the raw wording. 9) Checker hints: CCEL pages print footnotes inline; New Advent pages leave double spaces where footnote marks were removed; the archive.org texts are OCR with double spaces between words, so compare with whitespace collapsed.
